Q: Transfer binary file with CANopen A:

I worked with CANopen but binary transfers I only did with CAN so far.

Checking the CANopen cia 301 documents, I would go with the DOMAIN type, as it fits the problem well:

  • DOMAIN (Object code 2): Large variable amount of data e.g. executable program code.
  • Domains can be used to transfer an arbitrary large block of data from a client to a server and vice-versa. The contents of a data block is application specific.

The tutorial from canopennode has a "Demo domain" part with some examples.

Usually in a CANopen stack you then can react to a received object and start writing to eeprom etc.

Q: Converting a data set into a data frame A:

With {collapse}

collapse::unlist2d(l=df$x)

e.g.

> collapse::unlist2d(l=df$x)  |>  
+   head()
  .id Consumption    Income
1   1   1.2956003 1.3494292
2   1   0.8485697 1.3218216
3   1   0.3185874 0.1642931
4   1   1.5231161 1.3339185
5   1   0.7618668 1.1741444
6   2   0.8480480 2.3678244

With idcols-argument you can specify the name. {collapse} is generally considered a rapidfly fast package, it also ships collapse::pivot-function for reshaping.

With R's {base}

If the group column (.id) is not needed, simply

do.call(what='rbind', args=df$x) |> 
  as.data.frame()

If needed, I tend to use a Map + [<- construct like

lapply(df$x, data.frame) |> 
  ( \(.) Map(`[<-`, ., '.id', value=seq_along(df$x)) )() |> 
  do.call(what='rbind')

For wide format

lapply(df$x, data.frame) |> 
  do.call(what='cbind') |> 
  data.frame(check.names=TRUE)

might be enough.

Notes

  1. df <- <sth> masks stats::df- function which ships with R Core. From the head of the corresponding help file

FDist {stats} R Documentation The F Distribution Description Density, distribution function, quantile function and random generation for the F distribution with df1 and df2 degrees of freedom (and optional non-centrality parameter ncp). Usage df(x, df1, df2, ncp, log = FALSE) ...

Therefore, I recommend to assign to either metasyntactic variable names, e.g. foobar, foo, bar, baz, quux, xyzzy, ...,--personally I like .data, x, X which is rather R-specific--or something data-specific, e.g. cshd for cross-sectional household data.

  1. Where does the data come from. You might have an important issue and currently we are solving an XY-problem.

  2. Some tidy data references would encourage you to keep the data in long format.

Q: Creating clickable link to text file in Powershell A:

String replacement can be done using either the -replace $regex, $subst operator, or using the .Replace($string, $subst) method. The former takes a regex (so the input backslash needs to be escaped), the latter takes an ordinary string.

$withslashes = ($path -replace "\\", "/")

$withslashes = $path.Replace("\", "/")

Don't forget to URL-encode the path – that's necessary for paths which contain special characters:

$url = "file:///" + [uri]::EscapeUriString($path -replace "\\", "/")

$url = "file:///" + [uri]::EscapeUriString($path.Replace("\", "/"))

In this case it turns out that EscapeUriString keeps : and / as-is so it can be passed the whole path at once.

If it hadn't, then you could still encode each path component separately (which might be necessary in other programming languages):

"file:///" + (($path -split "\\" | % {[uri]::EscapeUriString($_)}) -join "/")

Note that the URL syntax is scheme: //host /path. For file: URLs, the host name should be left empty, but you still need the correct amount of slashes – 3 in total; two to indicate that the (empty) host follows and one to indicate that the path follows.

file:///C:/foo/bar

Example with host name to illustrate the syntax (file URLs with hostnames aren't allowed in general, but they get used in some special cases, like OSC 7 "current path" indications in terminals):

file://desktop-asdfgh/C:/foo/bar

It is also syntactically valid (though rare and not always supported) to leave out the //host part completely, keeping only a single slash to indicate that the /path follows – this is recognized by Windows Terminal, and also often seen in KDE:

file:/C:/foo/bar

But if you write file://C:/foo/bar, that would mean C: is the hostname. Some programs will understand it regardless, but some won't – Windows Terminal will not.

You can use OSC 8 sequences to make a link with custom text (supported by Windows Terminal and several others):

$ESC = [char] 0x1B

echo ("$ESC]8;;" + $url + "$ESC\" + "Hello" + "$ESC]8;;" + "$ESC\")

$ESC + "[" is CSI, $ESC + "]" is OSC, $ESC + "\" is ST (sequence terminator).

Q: Listing all descendants in Rails 8 A:

It seems a conceptual issue, there is already a loader in place managing my directory of interest, Rails.autoloaders.main and it is that which needs to be instructed to eager-load. I find by experimentation that adding the following to config/application.rb

config.after_initialize do
  Rails
    .autoloaders
    .main
    .eager_load_dir(Rails.root.join('app/components'))
end

ensures that ApplicationComponent.descendants returns the full list of subclasses in every environment but has no noticeable effect on startup time.
